\chapter{Inside the House}
\label{ch:hi-inside-the-house}
\hlchaptermodality{58}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five parts of a house when I greet someone at it.}

\section[dīvār]{\hi{दीवार} (dīvār) — a wall}

\label{lesson:HI-C58-wall}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did the last two words of the chapter before mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{दीवार}}
\textbf{\hi{दीवार}} (\emph{dīvār}) — \textquotedblleft{}a wall\textquotedblright{}.

A Persian word, \emph{dīvār}, 'wall'. Its older Iranian form was a compound, and the piece at the front of it is not certainly identified, so this book will name the Persian and stop there.

It is a loan and not a cousin, which is worth keeping straight: \hi{दरवाज़ा}, which you already own, is Persian too, and the two of them furnish most of the outside of a Hindi house between them.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five parts of the house.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dīvār}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{dīvār}, and \hi{दरवाज़ा} in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{दीवार} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a wall\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[chat]{\hi{छत} (chat) — a roof}

\label{lesson:HI-C58-roof}



\begin{quote}
What did the word before this one mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{छत}}
\textbf{\hi{छत}} (\emph{chat}) — \textquotedblleft{}a roof\textquotedblright{}.

From Sanskrit \hi{छत्र} (\emph{chatra}), which meant a parasol — the thing held over a person's head. The word came down off the handle and settled onto the building.

A flat \hi{छत} in North India is a place people go, not only a lid: it is where washing dries and where the evening is sat out. The word covers the surface and the use at once.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The second of five, and a parasol that turned into a roof.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{chat}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{chat}, over the \emph{dīvār}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \hi{छत} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a roof\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[khiṛkī]{\hi{खिड़की} (khiṛkī) — a window}

\label{lesson:HI-C58-window}



\begin{quote}
Name the 2 words of this chapter so far.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{खिड़की}}
\textbf{\hi{खिड़की}} (\emph{khiṛkī}) — \textquotedblleft{}a window\textquotedblright{}.

The origin of \hi{खिड़की} is not settled, and the derivations offered for it are guesses of varying quality rather than an agreed line.

This is the second time this book has had to say that about a piece of an ordinary house, and it will not be the last. A word being everywhere is no guarantee that its history was written down.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The third of five, and another honest gap.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[sīṛhī]{\hi{सीढ़ी} (sīṛhī) — a staircase, a ladder}

\label{lesson:HI-C58-stairs}



\begin{quote}
Name the 3 words of this chapter so far.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{सीढ़ी}}
\textbf{\hi{सीढ़ी}} (\emph{sīṛhī}) — \textquotedblleft{}a staircase, a ladder\textquotedblright{}.

\hi{सीढ़ी} is traced to a Sanskrit word for a flight of steps, but the exact form behind it is disputed and the sources differ on which one it was.

The word does not distinguish a staircase from a ladder. Both are \hi{सीढ़ी}, because what the word names is the going up, not the thing's construction.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The fourth of five, and one word for two objects.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{sīṛhī}, up to the \emph{chat}
\end{itemize}

\section[chādar]{\hi{चादर} (chādar) — a sheet}

\label{lesson:HI-C58-sheet}



\begin{quote}
Name the 4 words of this chapter so far.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \hi{चादर}}
\textbf{\hi{चादर}} (\emph{chādar}) — \textquotedblleft{}a sheet\textquotedblright{}.

Persian \emph{chādar}, a sheet or a veil — a single broad piece of cloth, whatever it is spread over. English borrowed it too, as \emph{chuddar}.

So it ends the chapter the way \hi{दीवार} began it: a Persian word for a plain domestic thing, taken whole. A Hindi house is furnished in two languages at once, and neither of them is hiding.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The fifth of five. That is the house, wall to roof.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\end{itemize}
